utterances.text: In fact, I was asking about the distinction between captured persons and arrested persons.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A person who is arrested is a person arrested normally in pre-indictment proceedings, and a captured person means somebody who was taken prisoner during combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The first category is subject to prosecution and the second category, if not guilty of a crime, is subject to an exchange?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you rephrase? Of course, people who were deprived of liberty were arrested in connection with a crime. Whether they are in custody or are serving a sentence, they fall under the category of arrested persons, detainees, and the other category are those captured in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that would include also Serbs, if they were caught fighting on the enemy side? In my first question, could the interpreters make this correction, I said "captured persons," not "convicts." Now, as a member of the government, you maybe heard of this, the Ministry of Health needed this information probably for the purposes of the International Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Probably.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May this be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D475, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now get 1D224. We won't dwell on it long. We just want to see how the chief of the Security Services Centre passes a document or an order on to public security stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: These terms may be confusing to foreigners, but a CSB covers several municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's a regional police centre, and public security stations are municipal police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't know if we have a translation for these, but is this the same document from the minister that Chief Zupljanin passes on to his subordinates?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes, you can see the text is the same.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, a portion of 05607 has the translation for this document as well as two other documents on the accused's list.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can I tender this? If the Chamber needs the English translation, I kindly ask for this to be displayed. But, in any case, let me point out this is the same document, order issued by the minister, and that I just wanted to show what the chief of the CSB is doing with this order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So it forms a series of forwarding the same order, Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI D476, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think Mr. Tieger said we have this translation, so it doesn't need to be MFI'd. Can we get 1D261.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We haven't checked whether we have a full translation. When it is verified, we can admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, and if there is no objection from the Prosecution, I would like to show on the ELMO one of my orders to the local civilian and municipal authorities that relates to this topic. It's a standing order without any date, and nobody can say that it's expired. This is, I think, a good time for Mr. Mandic to identify this document, if we can put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what this instruction means? It was issued to all the local police and civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know this document. It's your order and instruction to all local civilian and police authorities, which means local self-governments in municipalities, in the police: "Allow ICRC delegates to travel throughout the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina which is controlled by the Serbs. They are authorised to visit any and all prisons, including military camps and police stations under Serbian control. Therefore, all the troops of the Serbian forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina are required by you to facilitate the safe passage for ICRC delegates and vehicles. ICRC delegates shall prove their identity by producing Red Cross IDs and displaying the emblem of the Red Cross on their vehicles. "B. All measures should be taken to ensure that the Red Cross emblem is respected and to avoid any disturbance and/or attack on the vehicles and staff of the ICRC. All information related to prisoners should be provided and ICRC visits to prisons facilitated."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Minister, that we gave this to the representatives of the ICRC and that they could show it along with their ID cards at any check-point in order to be allowed to pass?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, this was used by them instead of a pass. This was a pass, actually, for them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May it be admitted or marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is there a date on this document? Can we see the top part of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no date, Your Honours, because it's a standing order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you remember when it was issued?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the early summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D477, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we have in e-court 65 ter 146. 146. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you identify these minutes?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are minutes from the session of the Presidency of Republika Srpska of the 30th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the agenda?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The agenda was: "The question of a pardon for Elvir Kesadzic, prisoner in the Manjaca camp; transfer of payments and financial transactions; report on war crimes against the Serbian people in the former Bosnia and Herzegovina --"

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. May we have page 3 of this document, please. I believe it's also page 3 in English. AD-5 is the passage we want.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In Serbian, we'll probably have to move on to the next page, but can you read where it says: "Commissioners and commissions ..."?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Commissioners and commissions must be introduced --" Oh, now it's gone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 3 back, please, in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Commissioners --"

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In English, it begins with: "Commissioners and commissions ..." Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "... must be introduced in areas where the civilian municipal authority is not functioning. A commissioner must bear personal responsibility. The question of army apartments and other property must be systematically resolved. Also there were objections to the work of the civilian authorities in the municipalities, and the conclusion was personnel changes are required in cases where this is justified, it must be made possible under the law to dismiss the municipal authorities."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But we don't see this in English. It's all in item 5 in English. We should put that back. It's the next page in English. It's a new page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you say: "It is necessary to make it legally possible for municipal authorities to be stripped of power." Can we have page 4 in Serbian. And while we are waiting for it to come up: Minister, is this evidence that in late November, the government was fed up with the self-will of the municipal authorities, or self-management, let me put it that way, the vestiges of the old regime? Yes, yes, the Presidency session, but this is probably at the request of the government.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you repeat your question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I simply wanted to ask you: Does this prove that in late November, the Presidency, probably at the initiative of the government, was dissatisfied with the way authority was passed down to municipal level?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we were still in the process of setting up the government authorities at that time, and that individual local authorities were out of control still.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you read and interpret page 4, please?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The issue of the role of deputies in those milieus in which they were elected was raised again. A deputy must carry out or implement the government authority in his area, and his work must be two-way between the people and the authority. Conclusion: "The status, rights, duties, powers and personal responsibilities of people's deputies must be regulated by special decision."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the Presidency here advocate influencing events on the ground through the people's deputies, which implies that prior to this, they did not have any influence on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the areas from which they were elected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you also agree that the president did not have any authority over deputies and could only ask them or appeal to them to act in this way?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a situation of an imminent threat of war, you had no legal power over the deputies.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D478, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we now have D92. It's already been admitted, but it's simply to refresh our memories as to how, in late July, the situation regarding minorities [Realtime transcript read in error "minors"] at Pale was developing. Can we now have page 16 in Serbian and page 21 in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While we are waiting for that: Mr. Mandic, when was it that you were sent to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In late 1992, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How late in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the 23rd of November, when Mr. Djeric resigned at the Assembly in Zvornik. So the date is the 23rd of November. After that, I was informed that I would continue working in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question was whether you were in Bosnia at the time of the previous Presidency meeting which we saw just now. It was dated as 30th of November.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was in Bosnia at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we now look at the minutes of this session. And it refers to minorities, not minors. I'm afraid that the transcript says "minors" rather than "minorities," so it's about the treatment of minorities. And it says here: "In Podrinje, the Muslims do not want peace, except in Bijeljina." In English, it says: "The Serbs and others live freely there." If you find the word "Podrinje" in the Serbian version -- can we scroll down in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it page 16?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, page 16, [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "The Serbs and others live freely there." We do have the text in English, but can we have the next page in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I must say that, sadly, the Muslims in Podrinje do not want peace, except in Bijeljina, in Pale, where they form 20 per cent of the population, where nobody bothers them or considers them to be second-class citizens. On the contrary, our government officials are communicating with them to persuade them that they have nothing to fear. Therefore, in Serb Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Serbs have accomplished their state, their freedom, and the state is big enough for all. I hope that at this Assembly session, we shall come to some conclusions and decisions to further strengthen this state."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that at Pale, the deputy prime minister -- the vice-president of the republic, Mr. Koljevic, was always at the disposal of the Muslims, whenever they wanted to come and talk to them, and that he kept telling them that they need not be afraid even though some Muslims elsewhere had killed their Serb neighbours?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that Mr. Koljevic spoke to them, but I do know for certain that Malko Koroman, the chief of police at Pale, was very concerned and very active in ensuring their safety and security.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does it say here also that they were living peacefully in Bijeljina, and that can be linked to the other document we saw, stating that Muslims were actually returning to Bijeljina when Mr. Panic and I called upon them to do so?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's stated here that in Bijeljina, the Muslims were living in peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell Their Honours what Podrinje is and what it has to do with the region of Birac?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Podrinje is a territory bordering with Serbia, along the Valley of the River Drina, from Foca to Bijeljina, the towns are Zvornik, Bratunac, Srebrenica, Ljubinje, Ljubija, Foca, Visegrad and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do I say here that in Podrinje, they don't want peace, except for Bijeljina, where they do want peace; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that along the River Drina, there is a small town called Janja, with a large Muslim community, and that it remained peaceful throughout the war, and that there was never any combat there or any fighting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Janja had a majority Muslim population both before the war and now. It's between Zvornik and Bijeljina, closer to Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This is already in evidence. May we now have 1D2031.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While we are waiting: Mr. Mandic, you didn't answer the question by the accused as to the relation between the region of Birac and Podrinje.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could he clarify the question? I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that Podrinje is a broader term and that part of it is the region of Birac, which we will show on the map tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I was explaining where the territory of Podrinje extends, it extends along the banks of the River Drina, from Foca to Bijeljina, and there are all these towns on the banks of the River Drina, Bijeljina, Janja, Zvornik, Bratunac, Srebrenica, Visegrad, Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And Gorazde; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and Gorazde, whereas Birac extends from Zvornik in the direction of Sarajevo, in the direction of Milici and Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Also Bratunac and Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it covers parts of the municipalities of Bratunac and Srebrenica. These are continental municipalities at the foot of Mount Romanija.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us about this document dated the 10th of September, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, you addressed the Main Staff of the Army of the Serb Republic, and you consider that we do not have the right to reject Muslim recruits and their desire to defend the Serbian Republic: "Furthermore, we find their desire to fight against the Croatian Ustasha, rather than on some other front, understandable. "Therefore, please ensure the proper political conditions for accepting these Muslim soldiers and treating them with dignity. Also, I do not think it is advisable to form a separate Muslim unit, but rather that they should be deployed in the existing units."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this is my response to a confidential telegram when the Main Staff asked me what they should do with those Muslims who wanted to fight, and here I agreed to their being accepted; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am not aware of what the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska wrote to you, but I do know that on the territory of Bijeljina, Janja, and Trebinje, there were soldiers in the Army of Republika Srpska who were of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I thought that separate units should not be established. But do you know that in some areas like Srbac, they did want to have their own unit, but until the end of the war they were part of our army?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I don't know how units were established and for how long they fought, but I do know that there were non-Serbs fighting in the Army of Republika Srpska. That, I can confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you also confirm there were also Croats who were officers at Pale, who remained there throughout the war and are still there to this day, living at Pale?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked you about positive discrimination. Do you agree that the Serbs had to respond to mobilisation, whereas Muslims and Croats were not obliged to do so, and if they did respond, we did not put them at lines where they would have to fight against their co-nationals, people of the same ethnicity; rather, we put them on other lines, because, as it says here, it was their desire -- it was their wish, which we considered to be natural?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, Mr. President. The deployment of non-Serbs in the Army of Republika Srpska is something I'm not familiar with.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D479, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D365. We don't have the Serbian version here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I show this to you because you will know how this agreement was implemented. I will read it out in English: [In English] "Between the Board of Deputies of British Jews and the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia." [No interpretation]: [In English] "The Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia, whereby permission is given to enable those members of the Jewish community living in Sarajevo, who wish to leave the city, to do so without any fear of harm, attack, or any other adverse consequence." [Interpretation] And here we can see the other points. May we have the last page, please. Thank you. [In English] "It is further agreed that members of the Jewish community who leave Sarajevo in this way be held the right to return and reclaim their properties. Their homes will be sealed and protected from invasion." [Interpretation] And this is signed in London on the 29th of July, 1992. Do you remember that the Sarajevo Jews left over our territory, whereas in the Serbian Republic they remained mainly in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the way in which these Jews were allowed to pass through the territory of Republika Srpska. This is the first time I have seen this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we did not publicise this, we didn't advertise it. But do you recall that Slovenes, Croats, and Muslims all left passing through our territory, and do you remember that the candidate for the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, representing others, was Mr. Ceresnjes, who was the leader of the Jewish community in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you didn't deal with politics, so we'll attend to this through some other witness on some other occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That's it for today. As regards the time for cross-examination of the coming witness, General Abdel-Razek, the Chamber has considered the following points: first, the limited period of time covered by the anticipated testimony of the witness, regarding broadly the same issues as the previous witness; two, the small number of associated exhibits with a few pages only, including some video material; third, the fact that the Prosecution requested one hour for examination-in-chief; and, number 4, in particular bearing in mind the fact that the witness can provide specific evidence about meetings with the accused and other alleged JCE members, in particular, Mrs. Biljana Plavsic and Nikola Koljevic. So although Mr. Karadzic asked for 14 hours for his cross-examination, the Chamber is of the view that a reasonable time for cross-examination of this particular witness should not exceed five hours. I hope this will be of assistance in your planning. We'll -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I may have misspoke earlier, without factoring in all the circumstances. So given the current circumstances, I can't think of an objection on our part to the proposed schedule for Monday. And I may have signaled otherwise, so I just wanted to make that clear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I learn until when I will be here tomorrow so that I can arrange my travel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We allowed the accused to have a further two hours tomorrow. That will be -- the first session will be closed -- will be concluded at 10.30, and after which he will have a half-an-hour break and he will have a further 30 minutes. So that means unless the Chamber -- any member of the Chamber has a question for you, you will be free to leave around 11.30, at least before noon tomorrow. Thank you, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll resume at 9.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 16th day of July, 2010, at 9.00 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
